question.prompt: The number of distinct lines representing the altitudes, medians, and interior angle bisectors of a triangle that is isosceles, but not equilateral, is:

solutions.explanation:
Let \(AB=AC\), so \(A\) is the apex and \(BC\) is the base. There are three named lines at each vertex, making nine before coincidences are considered. In an isosceles triangle, the altitude, median, and interior angle bisector from the apex all lie on one line. Thus the apex contributes just one distinct line.

We must check that no further coincidences reduce the count. At any vertex, coincidence of any two of these three lines forces the two adjacent sides to be equal:

• An altitude that is also a median is the perpendicular bisector of the opposite side, so its vertex is equally distant from that side's endpoints.

• An altitude that is also an interior angle bisector divides the triangle into two right triangles with a common leg and equal angles at the original vertex. These triangles are congruent, so the adjacent sides are equal.

• An interior angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides. If it is also a median, the divided pieces are equal, so the adjacent sides are equal.

At \(B\), such a coincidence would give \(BA=BC\). Together with \(AB=AC\), this would make the triangle equilateral, which is excluded. The same argument applies at \(C\). Thus each base vertex contributes three different lines.

Finally, a line associated with two different vertices would have to be the side joining them. A median or interior angle bisector cannot be a side. Nor can a side be an altitude from both its endpoints: the other two sides would then both be perpendicular to it and hence parallel, which is impossible in a triangle.

There are therefore exactly
\[
1+3+3=\boxed{7}
\]
distinct lines, choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Count the coincident lines
